slides.narration: How can people of many faiths live together as equals? In this part we meet two kinds of religious domination, define secularism, and compare two models of how a state can relate to religion.

slides.heading: Two kinds of religious domination

rows: A Sunhold trust keeps the Tessel community out of the market hall in Ashvale
Domination within a religious community, for example by caste or gender
A Rivermark council bars women from reading aloud at its gatherings in Quillfield

visual.caption: The towns, faiths and councils are imagined.

slides.narration: Inter religious domination means one religious community dominating another. Intra religious domination means domination within a community, for example by caste or gender. In the imagined town of Ashvale a Sunhold trust keeps the Tessel community out of a hall. In Quillfield a Rivermark council bars women from reading aloud.

visual.alt: Chart of the two kinds of religious domination. Inter-religious domination is one community dominating another, between communities, for example an imagined Sunhold trust keeping the Tessel community out of a market hall in the town of Ashvale. Intra-religious domination is domination inside one community, by caste or gender for example, such as an imagined Rivermark council barring women from reading aloud at its gatherings in the town of Quillfield. Secularism opposes both kinds: freedom within religions, equality between them, and state power kept apart from the control of any religious group
visual.caption: Two kinds of religious domination, with imagined examples.

slides.narration: This chart sets the two kinds side by side. Between communities, one dominates another. Within a community, some members dominate others, by caste or gender for example. Secularism opposes both. It seeks freedom within religions and equality between them, and keeps state power apart from the control of any religious group.

slides.heading: The standard definition of secularism

rows: A normative doctrine that seeks a society free from both inter-religious and intra-religious domination
Freedom within religions and equality between them
What it needs of the state
State power kept apart from the control of any religious group
It states how things ought to be, and not only how they are

visual.alt: Table on the standard definition of secularism: a normative doctrine that seeks a society free from both inter-religious and intra-religious domination; it promotes freedom within religions and equality between them; state power is kept apart from the control of any religious group; normative means it states how things ought to be

slides.narration: Secularism is a normative doctrine that seeks a society free from both inter religious and intra religious domination. Normative means that it states how things ought to be. It promotes freedom within religions and equality between them, and it keeps state power apart from the control of any religious group.

visual.caption: The statements and the town are imagined.

slides.narration: Let us classify four imagined statements in Ashvale. A hall committee of one faith refuses a hall to another. That is inter religious. A council forbids its own women to lead prayers. That is intra religious, by gender. An elder fines families who dine with other hereditary groups of the same faith. That is intra religious. A trust lets only its own processions use the main street. That is inter religious.

slides.heading: What a secular state is

rows: Not run by any religious group
Religious leaders or bodies do not hold state power as such
The state does not name any religion as its own
No discrimination on grounds of religion
Citizens are treated alike whatever faith they follow
Meridan names the Sunhold faith its official religion; it cannot be called secular in this sense

visual.alt: Table of features of a secular state: not run by any religious group; no official religion; no discrimination on grounds of religion; imagined contrast, Meridan names the Sunhold faith its official religion and cannot be called secular in this sense
visual.caption: Meridan is imagined.

slides.narration: A secular state is not run by any religious group. It has no official religion. And it does not discriminate against anyone on grounds of religion. In the imagined country of Meridan the Sunhold faith is named the official religion, so Meridan cannot be called secular in this sense.

slides.heading: The Western model

rows: Mutual exclusion: the state does not interfere in religion and religion does not interfere in the state
Little room for rights based on a community
The United States and France, which differ from each other in detail
Calendra gives no grant to any religious body and no religious body takes part in lawmaking

visual.alt: Table on the Western model as commonly taught: mutual exclusion, the state does not interfere in religion and religion does not interfere in the state; focus on individual freedom and equality; little room for community rights; the United States and France are often given as examples and differ in detail; imagined Calendra gives no grant to any religious body and no religious body takes part in lawmaking
visual.caption: Calendra is imagined.

slides.narration: In the Western model, as it is commonly taught, the state does not interfere in religion and religion does not interfere in the state. This is called mutual exclusion. The focus is on individual freedom and equality, and there is little room for rights based on a community. The United States and France are often given as examples, though they differ in detail.

slides.heading: The Indian model

rows: Principled distance: the state keeps a distance from all religions but may intervene on principle
All religions are respected, and communities are supported on an equal footing

visual.alt: Table on the Indian model: principled distance, the state keeps a distance from all religions but may intervene on principle; the aim of intervention is to promote freedom and equality; equal respect for all religions and support for communities on an equal footing; freedom of religion in Articles 25 to 28; no state religion

slides.narration: The Indian model rests on principled distance. The state keeps a distance from all religions but may intervene, on principle, to promote freedom and equality. All religions receive equal respect, and communities are supported on an equal footing. Freedom of religion is protected in Articles twenty five to twenty eight, and there is no state religion.

A secular state has no official religion and does not discriminate on grounds of religion.

slides.heading: Principled distance

rows: A distance from all religions, with intervention allowed on principle
Freedom and equality of people, within and between communities
Abolition of untouchability (Article 17); opening places of worship to all castes
Minorities may run educational institutions (Article 30), with all communities on an equal footing

visual.alt: Table on principled distance: a distance from all religions, with intervention allowed on principle; the principle is freedom and equality of people within and between communities; intervention example is abolition of untouchability under Article 17 and opening places of worship to all castes; support example is Article 30 for minority educational institutions; the term is associated with the political theorist Rajeev Bhargava

slides.narration: Principled distance means a distance from all religions, with intervention allowed on principle. The principle is the freedom and equality of people, within and between communities. The state acted against untouchability under Article seventeen, and places of worship were opened to all castes. Article thirty lets minorities run educational institutions. The term is associated with the theorist Rajeev Bhargava.

slides.narration: To sum up. Religious domination is inter religious or intra religious. Secularism seeks a society free from both. The Indian model is principled distance with equal respect. The word secular was added in nineteen seventy six.

visual.alt: Chart of six criticisms of Indian secularism and the replies. Anti-religious: critics say it is hostile to religion; supporters respond that it opposes domination, not religion, and freedom of religion is protected. A Western import: critics say it is borrowed from elsewhere; supporters respond that it grew from India's own diversity and differs from the Western model. Minoritism: critics say it favours minorities; supporters respond that minority rights protect the vulnerable and are part of equal respect. Interventionist: critics say it interferes in communities; supporters respond that intervention promotes equality and freedom, as with untouchability. Vote-bank politics: critics say it rewards groups for votes; supporters respond that groups organising is part of democracy and the concern is neglect of others. An impossible project: critics say differences run too deep; supporters respond that it is an ambitious ideal that keeps societies together and partial success counts

sections.body_md:
In a society with many faiths, one community may **dominate** another, and members of one community may dominate others inside it.

- **Inter-religious domination**: one religious community dominating another.
- **Intra-religious domination**: domination within a religious community, for example by caste or gender.

sections.heading: 2. Meaning of secularism and the secular state
sections.body_md:
**Secularism** is a **normative doctrine** that seeks a society free from both inter-religious and intra-religious domination. It promotes **freedom within religions** and **equality between** them, and keeps state power apart from the control of any religious group.

A **secular state** is not run by any religious group, has **no official religion** and does **not discriminate** on grounds of religion.

sections.heading: 3. The Western model
sections.body_md: As commonly taught, the Western model rests on **mutual exclusion**: the state does not interfere in religion and religion does not interfere in the state. It focuses on **individual freedom and equality** and leaves little room for **community-based rights**. The United States and France are often given as examples; they differ from each other in detail.

key_terms.definition_md: The idea that the state does not interfere in religion and religion does not interfere in the state.

sections.heading: 4. The Indian model and principled distance
sections.body_md:
The Indian model rests on **principled distance**: the state keeps a distance from all religions but may **intervene on principle** to promote freedom and equality. Examples are the abolition of untouchability (**Article 17**) and the opening of places of worship to all castes.

It also gives **equal respect** to all religions and supports communities on an equal footing, as with **Article 30**. There is **no state religion**. The term principled distance is associated with the political theorist Rajeev Bhargava.

key_terms.definition_md: The state keeps a distance from all religions but may intervene on principle to promote freedom and equality.
Treating every religion and community with the same regard, with support given on an equal footing.

sections.heading: 5. The Constitution and secularism
sections.body_md:
The Constitution was **secular in its provisions from the start**. **Article 15** bars discrimination on grounds of religion. **Article 17** abolishes untouchability. **Articles 25 to 28** protect freedom of religion. **Article 30** lets religious and linguistic minorities set up and run educational institutions.

The word **secular** was added to the Preamble by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.

key_terms.definition_md: The amendment of 1976 that added the word secular to the Preamble.

rows: Describes India as secular; the word was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976
No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
Abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice
Freedom of religion, management of religious affairs, no tax for promoting a religion, and a rule on religious instruction in institutions wholly funded by the state
Religious and linguistic minorities may set up and run educational institutions of their choice
The Constitution was secular in its provisions from 1950; the Preamble word came later

sections.heading: 6. Criticisms of Indian secularism, with replies (1)
sections.body_md:
**Anti-religious.** Critics have argued that it is hostile to religion. Supporters respond that it opposes **domination, not religion**.

**A Western import.** Critics have argued that it comes from elsewhere. Others argue that it grew from India's **own conditions of diversity** and differs from the Western model.

**Minoritism.** Critics have argued that it favours minorities. Supporters respond that **minority rights protect vulnerable groups** and are part of equal respect, and that fundamental interests deserve protection.

key_terms.definition_md: The criticism that Indian secularism favours minorities.

sections.body_md:
**Interventionist.** Critics have argued that the state interferes in communities. Supporters respond that intervention promotes **equality and freedom**, as with untouchability. Debates on personal laws exist, and people hold different views on them.

**Vote-bank politics.** Critics have argued that communities are promised favours for votes. Supporters respond that groups organising for their interests is part of **democracy**; the concern is when others are **neglected**.

**An impossible project.** Critics have argued that differences run too deep. Supporters respond that it is an **ambitious ideal** that keeps diverse societies together, and **partial success** is still valuable.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying secularism means opposing religion: say it opposes domination, between and within religions.
- Describing only inter-religious domination: include intra-religious domination.
- Saying the Indian state keeps total separation: say principled distance allows intervention on principle for freedom and equality.
- Saying the word secular was in the Constitution only from 1976: the word was added in 1976, the provisions were secular from the start.
- Giving a criticism without its reply, or taking a side without reasons.
- Naming a party or a real event: use an imagined example.

**Tips:** define with both kinds of domination; use the phrases critics have argued and supporters respond; cite Articles by number; weigh both sides, then judge with reasons.

Stating how things ought to be, and not only how they are.

cards.front_md: Which countries are often given as examples of the Western model?

The idea that state and religion do not interfere in each other.

No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

cards.back_md: Anti-religious, a Western import, minoritism, interventionist, vote-bank politics and an impossible project.

questions.stem_md: Political theorists describe secularism as a normative doctrine. What does this doctrine seek?

options.text_md: A society in which every person follows one common faith
A society free from both inter-religious and intra-religious domination
A society in which religion is wiped out of private life
A society in which the state adopts the faith of its largest community

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A society free from both inter-religious and intra-religious domination. Secularism seeks a society free from domination between religious communities and within them. It does not ask for one common faith, the removal of religion from private life or a state faith.

questions.stem_md: Which pair correctly explains the two kinds of religious domination?

options.text_md: Inter-religious domination happens only in cities; intra-religious domination happens only in villages
Inter-religious domination is domination by the state; intra-religious domination is domination by a court
Inter-religious domination is a duty of citizens; intra-religious domination is a right of citizens
Inter-religious domination is one community dominating another; intra-religious domination is domination inside a community, for example by caste or gender

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Inter-religious domination is one community dominating another; intra-religious domination is domination inside a community, for example by caste or gender. The prefix tells the difference: inter means between communities and intra means within one community. Place of living, the state and a court, or duties and rights, have nothing to do with the two kinds.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Ashvale, the committee that runs the old market hall allows only Sunhold festivals to be held there and turns away the Tessel community each time it applies. This is an example of

options.text_md: inter-religious domination
intra-religious domination
principled distance
mutual exclusion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** inter-religious domination. One community is using its hold over a shared hall to shut out another, which is inter-religious domination. Intra-religious domination is inside one community, and principled distance and mutual exclusion are models of the state's relation to religion.

questions.stem_md: The elders of the Rivermark community in the imagined town of Quillfield decide that women of the community may not read aloud at its gatherings, though men may. This is mainly an example of

options.text_md: inter-religious domination
a state interfering in religion
intra-religious domination based on gender
equal respect for all religions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** intra-religious domination based on gender. The restriction is placed on women by their own community, so the domination is inside one religion and rests on gender. No second community is involved, and no state action or equal respect appears in the case.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Dunmere, families of the Ostler group, a hereditary group within the Rivermark community, are not allowed to draw water from the well kept by the other groups of the same community. This is a case of

options.text_md: inter-religious domination
freedom of religion
intra-religious domination based on caste-like hereditary groups
a minority right to run schools

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** intra-religious domination based on caste-like hereditary groups. The exclusion is practised inside one religious community on the basis of birth into a group, which is intra-religious domination. Inter-religious domination needs two communities, and the case shows neither freedom of religion nor a school right.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a feature of a secular state?

options.text_md: It is not run by any religious group and has no official religion
It is run by the leaders of one religion
It names one religion as the state religion
It treats the followers of different religions by different laws of citizenship

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is not run by any religious group and has no official religion. A secular state is not controlled by any religious group, has no official religion and does not discriminate on grounds of religion. The other options describe states under religious rule, a state religion or discrimination.

questions.stem_md: The imagined country of Meridan declares the Sunhold faith its official religion, funds only Sunhold schools and opens its parliament with Sunhold prayers. Can Meridan be called a secular state in the standard sense?

options.text_md: Yes, because most people there follow the Sunhold faith
Yes, because it allows other faiths to exist
Yes, because the funding of schools never affects secularism
No, because a secular state has no official religion and does not favour any religious group

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** No, because a secular state has no official religion and does not favour any religious group. A secular state has no official religion and keeps state power apart from the control of any religious group, which Meridan does not do. The size of a community and bare permission for other faiths do not make a state secular.

questions.stem_md: The imagined country of Torvia refuses to give a public post to Janne because she follows the Tessel faith. Which principle of a secular state does this break?

options.text_md: The state must hold a census of faiths
The state does not discriminate against anyone on grounds of religion
The state must give every citizen a post
The state must fund every religious festival

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The state does not discriminate against anyone on grounds of religion. Refusing a post because of the applicant's religion is discrimination on a ground of religion, which a secular state does not practise. A census, a post for every person and funding for festivals are not part of that principle.

questions.stem_md: The model of secularism commonly taught as Western, with the United States and France given as examples, rests mainly on

options.text_md: mutual exclusion: the state does not interfere in religion and religion does not interfere in the state
principled distance, with the state free to intervene to promote equality
the rule of one state religion
the support of every community on an equal footing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** mutual exclusion: the state does not interfere in religion and religion does not interfere in the state. The Western model is described as mutual exclusion of state and religion. Principled distance and equal support belong to the Indian model, and a state religion has no place in a secular model.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined country of Calendra, the state gives no grant to any religious institution, takes no part in the affairs of any religion, and no religious body takes part in making laws. Which model does Calendra follow?

options.text_md: Principled distance, as in the Indian model
Mutual exclusion, as in the Western model
A state religion
Rule by a religious body

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Mutual exclusion, as in the Western model. A state and religion kept apart from each other on both sides is mutual exclusion. Principled distance allows the state to intervene on principle, and a state religion or religious rule would end the separation.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Western model, as commonly taught, said to leave little room for community-based rights?

options.text_md: Because it gives special powers to religious communities
Because it forbids every citizen to practise a religion
Because it centres on the freedom and equality of the individual
Because it needs a state religion to work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Because it centres on the freedom and equality of the individual. The model, as commonly taught, centres on individual freedom and equality, so rights held by a community as such find little place in it. It does not give communities special powers, forbid religion or need a state religion.

questions.stem_md: In the Indian model of secularism, principled distance means that the state

options.text_md: never has anything to do with any religion in any way
supports the religion of the largest community
controls the affairs of all religious communities
keeps a distance from all religions but may intervene, on principle, to promote freedom and equality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** keeps a distance from all religions but may intervene, on principle, to promote freedom and equality. Principled distance is a distance from every religion, with intervention allowed when the principles of freedom and equality call for it. Total separation, support for one religion and control of all communities are different ideas.

questions.stem_md: The imagined country of Torvia passes a law that every shrine open to the public must admit people of all hereditary groups, while the law leaves the conduct of worship to each shrine. This best shows

options.text_md: mutual exclusion, since the state is not involved
a state religion for Torvia
inter-religious domination
principled distance: intervention only to promote equality, while keeping away from belief and ritual

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** principled distance: intervention only to promote equality, while keeping away from belief and ritual. The state steps in on a matter of equality and keeps away from belief and ritual, which is principled distance. In mutual exclusion it would not step in, and the law favours no religion and ends domination inside a community.

questions.stem_md: Which Article of the Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice?

options.text_md: Article 25
Article 30
Article 17
Article 28

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Article 17. Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Article 25 concerns freedom of religion, Article 30 the educational institutions of minorities, and Article 28 religious instruction in certain institutions.

questions.stem_md: A student says that India became a secular state only in 1976. Which reply is correct?

options.text_md: The student is right, because there was no provision on religion before 1976
The word secular was added to the Preamble in 1976, but the Constitution was secular in its provisions from the start
The word secular appeared first in 1950 and was removed in 1976
The Constitution became secular by a vote of the Supreme Court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The word secular was added to the Preamble in 1976, but the Constitution was secular in its provisions from the start. The 1976 amendment added the word to the Preamble, while provisions such as those on freedom of religion and equal treatment were in the Constitution from the beginning. The other replies misstate this history.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Torvia gives each of its three main faiths the same sum to repair its place of worship if it is damaged by a flood. Which feature of the Indian model does this resemble?

options.text_md: Equal respect for all religions, with support given on an equal footing
Strict separation with no help to any religion
Preference for the oldest faith
Control of worship by the state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Equal respect for all religions, with support given on an equal footing. Help of the same kind on the same terms to every faith reflects equal respect and equal footing. Strict separation would give no help, and neither preference for one faith nor state control of worship is shown.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Pellmoor, the Teshar community opens Ember School to teach its own language and traditions, and the authorities recognise it on the same terms as other schools. Which Indian constitutional provision is closest to this arrangement?

options.text_md: Article 17, on untouchability
Article 30, on the educational institutions of minorities
Article 27, on taxes for a religion
Article 28, on religious instruction in wholly state-funded institutions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Article 30, on the educational institutions of minorities. The right of a community to run its own educational institutions on equal terms is what Article 30 provides. Article 17 is on untouchability, Article 27 on taxes and Article 28 on instruction in institutions wholly funded by the state.

questions.stem_md: Two councillors in Torvia argue about a shrine that refuses entry to a hereditary group. Councillor Brannoch says the state has no business inside any religion at all. Councillor Selka says the state may act, because the issue is equality. Whose view is closer to the Indian model?

options.text_md: Brannoch's, since the Indian model forbids all intervention
Both are equally close
Neither, since the Indian model supports the state religion
Selka's, since principled distance allows intervention to promote equality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Selka's, since principled distance allows intervention to promote equality. The Indian model keeps a distance but allows principled intervention for equality, which is Selka's view. Brannoch's view is closer to mutual exclusion. The Indian model has no state religion.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined town, a Tessel council fines members who marry outside their hereditary group, and a Sunhold trust refuses a hall for a Tessel wedding. Which description is correct?

options.text_md: The first is intra-religious domination and the second is inter-religious domination
The first is inter-religious domination and the second is intra-religious domination
Both are intra-religious domination
Neither is a kind of religious domination

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The first is intra-religious domination and the second is inter-religious domination. The fine is imposed inside one community, so it is intra-religious. The refusal of a hall by one community to another is inter-religious. The other options mix them up or deny both.

questions.stem_md: Critics say Indian secularism is anti-religious. What do supporters respond?

options.text_md: It is indeed meant to end all religion
It is meant to rank religions by merit
It opposes domination, not religion, and protects the freedom to follow a faith
It has nothing to say about religious freedom

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It opposes domination, not religion, and protects the freedom to follow a faith. Supporters point out that the target is domination, whether between or within religions, and that freedom of religion is protected. They do not accept that it aims to end religion or to rank faiths.

questions.stem_md: Critics call Indian secularism a Western import. Which reply do supporters offer?

options.text_md: It is a copy of the Western model with no changes
The place where an idea began decides whether it is valid
It grew out of India's own conditions of deep diversity and differs from the Western model, for example in principled distance
India has no diversity of religions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It grew out of India's own conditions of deep diversity and differs from the Western model, for example in principled distance. Supporters argue that the Indian model answers India's own diversity and has features, such as principled distance and community support, unlike the Western model. A copy, the origin test and denial of diversity do not answer the critics.

questions.stem_md: Critics say Indian secularism favours minorities. Which reply do supporters offer?

options.text_md: Minority rights protect vulnerable groups and form part of equal respect; fundamental interests deserve protection
Minorities should have more rights than any other group
Only larger communities need rights
Rights of any group should be removed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Minority rights protect vulnerable groups and form part of equal respect; fundamental interests deserve protection. Supporters argue that rights for minorities guard groups that could be vulnerable and are part of treating all with equal respect. They do not argue for superior status, rights only for large groups or the removal of rights.

questions.stem_md: Critics call Indian secularism interventionist. Which reply do supporters offer?

options.text_md: The state should intervene in everything a community does
The state does not intervene in any matter
Intervention is always wrong, so no law should ever be made
The state intervenes to promote equality and freedom, as in ending untouchability, and not out of hostility to a community

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The state intervenes to promote equality and freedom, as in ending untouchability, and not out of hostility to a community. Supporters hold that intervention is meant to promote freedom and equality, as with untouchability. They do not say the state may control everything, that it never intervenes or that no law may be made.

questions.stem_md: Vote-bank politics, as the criticism describes it, means

options.text_md: a bank in which voters keep their money
seeking the votes of a community by promising favours to it, so that other groups may be neglected
an election held only in banks
a rule that every voter must belong to a party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** seeking the votes of a community by promising favours to it, so that other groups may be neglected. Vote-bank politics is the seeking of a community's votes by promising it favours, with the worry that others are then neglected. The other statements have no connection with the term.

questions.stem_md: Which reply to the vote-bank criticism is the most balanced?

options.text_md: Groups organising to press for their interests is a normal part of democracy; the real concern arises when this leads to others being neglected
No group should ever organise
Neglect of other groups is acceptable if votes are gained
Democracy has no place for communities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Groups organising to press for their interests is a normal part of democracy; the real concern arises when this leads to others being neglected. A balanced reply accepts that groups press for their interests in a democracy while keeping the concern about neglect in view. Banning all organising, accepting neglect or excluding communities does not do so.

questions.stem_md: Critics call secularism an impossible project because religious differences run deep. What do supporters respond?

options.text_md: It has already succeeded completely
It is an ambitious ideal that helps keep diverse societies together, and partial success is still valuable
It should be dropped because it is hard
It does not matter whether societies stay together

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is an ambitious ideal that helps keep diverse societies together, and partial success is still valuable. Supporters admit that the ideal is hard but say it helps diverse societies live together and that partial success is worth having. Claiming complete success or dropping the ideal does not answer the critics.

questions.stem_md: At a public meeting in the imagined town of Ashvale a speaker says: the state keeps stepping into how communities arrange their own affairs. Which criticism of Indian secularism is she making?

options.text_md: That it is anti-religious
That it is a Western import
That it is interventionist
That it is impossible

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** That it is interventionist. Complaining that the state keeps stepping into the affairs of communities is the interventionist criticism. The anti-religious criticism says it is hostile to religion, the import criticism speaks of its origin, and the impossibility criticism says it cannot be achieved.

questions.stem_md: Rafe writes to the Quillfield Post: secularism is an idea that came from far-off lands and does not suit our ways. Which criticism does his letter state?

options.text_md: That it is minoritist
That it encourages vote-bank politics
That it is interventionist
That it is a Western import

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** That it is a Western import. Saying the idea came from elsewhere and does not suit local ways is the Western-import criticism. The other criticisms speak of favours, votes or intervention.

questions.stem_md: Nell is asked to judge the criticism that Indian secularism is anti-religious. Which approach is the best?

options.text_md: Agree with the critics without giving reasons
Ignore the criticism
Reject the criticism without reading it
State the criticism, give the supporters' reply that the target is domination and not religion, then judge with reasons and examples

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** State the criticism, give the supporters' reply that the target is domination and not religion, then judge with reasons and examples. A sound evaluation states the criticism, presents the reply and then judges with reasons and examples. Agreeing, ignoring or rejecting without reasons is not evaluation.

questions.stem_md: An editorial in an imagined paper says that since no country has removed religious domination completely, secularism should be given up. Which response is the best?

options.text_md: The editorial is right, since an ideal must be reached fully
No ideal has any value
An ideal can be worth pursuing even if it is only partly reached, as progress against domination still helps many people
Domination does not exist

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** An ideal can be worth pursuing even if it is only partly reached, as progress against domination still helps many people. The best reply is that partial progress against domination still helps people and keeps diverse societies together. Demanding full success, denying the value of ideals or denying domination does not meet the argument.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined state of Torvia, a parent complains that the Teshar community has a school protected by the constitution, while her own children have none such. Which reply best reflects the supporters' view?

options.text_md: The Teshar school must be closed
The protection is for a group that could be vulnerable and is part of equal respect; the concern about her own children can be examined on its merits
Her own community has no rights
Schools should never be protected by a constitution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The protection is for a group that could be vulnerable and is part of equal respect; the concern about her own children can be examined on its merits. Supporters would say that protections for minorities guard vulnerable groups and form part of equal respect, while a fair hearing for the parent's concern remains possible. Closing the school, denying her rights or banning protection are not part of that view.

questions.stem_md: A Torvian elder says: our council made its rule on dining long ago, and the state has no right to say that all groups may sit together. What do supporters of the Indian model reply?

options.text_md: Where a practice denies equality and dignity to people, principled intervention to promote equality is justified
The state may never touch any practice
The state should ban all dining rules of every kind
The elder is right in every case

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Where a practice denies equality and dignity to people, principled intervention to promote equality is justified. Supporters hold that when a practice denies equality and dignity, the state may intervene on principle. They do not hold that it may never act, that it should regulate everything, or that every practice is protected.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Secularism, in the standard sense, is concerned with domination inside religions as well as between them.

**Reason (R):** Domination within a religious community, for example by caste or gender, is a form of religious domination.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since domination inside a community counts as religious domination, a doctrine against religious domination must cover it too.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A state that names an official religion cannot be called secular in the standard sense.

**Reason (R):** A secular state has no official religion and is not run by any religious group.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
